abstract: Abstract Background Changes in the stratum corneum ( SC ) lipid profiles are associated with various skin diseases. Factors, including age, ethnicity, season and anatomical location, can influence the variations in SC lipid profiles. According to reports, the facial sebum of Chinese women peaks at age 20–30, accompanied by various signs of facial ageing. No studies have investigated how facial SC lipid profiles change with age in young Chinese women. Objectives This study aimed to observe the differences in the facial SC lipid profiles of Chinese female volunteers aged 19 – 33 and determined the relationship between key lipids and physiological parameters. Methods Differential lipids were detected and screened in healthy Chinese women aged 19 – 33 through ultra‐performance liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry. The relationship between these lipids and the skin's physiological parameters was determined. Results The facial SC lipid profiles of young Chinese women exhibited significant differences with age. The results indicated that 40 lipids increased with age, while 51 types decreased. The average chain length of diglycerides (DG), triglycerides (TG) and short‐chain ceramides decreased with age, while cholesterol esters (CE) and ceramides {Cer, Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0) and Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0)} increased with age. Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0), Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) and HexCer/NDS (d14:0/33:1) were positively correlated with trans‐epidermal water loss, skin elasticity and skin brightness, while Cer/AP (t18:0/20:0) was negatively correlated with skin elasticity. This study comprehensively explains the differences in lipid profile composition and skin ageing in young populations. Conclusions Young Chinese women's facial skin SC lipid profiles significantly change with age. Age‐related changes result in variations in DG and CE levels and changes in the chain lengths of TG and Cer. Age‐related changes in Cer content affect skin barrier function, elasticity and brightness.

Inclusion criteria
Female participants aged 19–33 years
Participants with self‐reported facial perceived age consistent with biological age
Daily life personnel without either special working and living environment (exposure to sunlight and night work) or specific intervention measures
Participants in good health at the time of assessment
Individuals who voluntarily consented to participate and signed the informed consent document

Exclusion criteria
Women who are planning to conceive, currently pregnant, breastfeeding, or have given birth within the past 6 months
Individuals suffering from severe systemic illnesses, immunodeficiencies or autoimmune disorders
Participants with a documented history of allergic reactions or those who have experienced allergies to cosmetic products within the previous 1–2 years
Individuals involved in other clinical trials either currently or within the preceding month
Participants exhibiting dermatological issues in the test area or those undergoing treatment
Individuals with medical conditions (including cold and flu) that may affect the outcomes of the study
Participants who were considered unsuitable for participation by the dermatologist
Measurement of skin physiological parameters
Participants were acclimatized for 30 min in a controlled environment with a temperature of 22 ± 1°C and humidity of 50 ± 5% before conducting skin assessments. Each participant underwent a series of tests, including skin complexion, elasticity, moisture content and trans‐epidermal water loss (TEWL) assessments on one randomized cheek, alongside sebum content measurement on the forehead.
Skin colour metrics were recorded using a CM2500d chromameter (CR‐400, Konica Minolta, Japan) and a Mexameter (MX18, Courage and Khazaka, Germany), which provided indices including L*, a*, b*, individual typology angle (ITA°), melanin index (MI) and erythema index (EI). Skin elasticity was evaluated using a Cutometer (Cutometer MPA 580; Courage and Khazaka, Germany), with parameters including Q0, R0, R2, R5 and R7. The hydration level of SC was measured with a Corneometer (Corneometer CM 825; Courage and Khazaka, Germany). TEWL and sebum were measured using the Vapometer (SWL5201, Delfin, Finland) and Sebumeter (SM815, Courage and Khazaka, Germany). The tested regions corresponding to various skin physiological parameters are presented in Figure
1
.

Schematic diagram of the test regions. (a) Skin sebum; (b) Melanin index, erythema index and elasticity; (c) Skin hydration, TEWL and colour (L*, b* and ITA°); (d) Skin patch sampling.
Lipid collection and preparation
Lipid collection was carried out and adjusted for the conditions described by Sadowski et al [
1
] A D‐Squame stripping disc (D101) was pressed on the sampling site for 10 s to collect the sample and then transferred to a tube. Samples were taken from the cheek in layers until the fifth layer was reached. Samples were stored at −80°C until extraction. The sites for skin patch sampling are illustrated in Figure
1
.

‐
MS
/
MS
analysis
Lipid extraction
Samples were retrieved from the −80°C freezer, mixed with 400 μL of water, and vortexed for 30 s. The mixture was then subjected to liquid nitrogen freezing for 1 min, followed by thawing. This freeze–thaw cycle was repeated 2–3 times. Subsequently, 960 μL of extraction solvent (MTBE: MeOH = 5:1, containing internal standard) was added, mixed, and subjected to another round of ultrasound for 10 min. The mixture was stored at −40°C for 1 h, followed by centrifugation at 4°C for 15 min at 3000 rpm (900 × g). The supernatant was collected, dried under vacuum, and reconstituted in 200 μL of solvent (DCM:MeOH = 1:1) for further analysis. The final mixture was vortexed for 30 s and centrifuged at 13000 rpm (16 200 × g) for 15 min, and 75 μL of the supernatant was transferred to a loading vial for testing.
UPLC‐MS/MS
UPLC‐MS/MS analysis is based on Xiahou et al.'s method [
18
] with minor modifications. Lipid compounds were analysed using a Vanquish ultrahigh‐performance liquid chromatograph (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and a Waters ACQUITY UPLC HSST3 (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.8 m) column. Mobile phase A was composed of 40% water and 60% acetonitrile, and 10 mol/L ammonium formate was added. Mobile phase B was composed of 10% acetonitrile and 90% isopropanol, and 50 mL of a 10 mmol/L ammonium formate aqueous solution was added to 1000 mL of B‐phase. The gradient elution was carried out as follows: 0–1.0 min at 40% B; 1.0–12.0 min transitioning from 40% to 100% B; 12.0–13.5 min at 100% B; 13.5–13.7 min transitioning back to 40% B; and 13.7–18.0 min at 40% B. The flow rate was maintained at 0.3 mL/min, with the column temperature set at 55°C and the sample plate at 4°C, utilizing a sampling volume of 2 μL for both positive and negative ion modes.
Mass spectrometric data was acquired through a Thermo Q Exactive HFX mass spectrometer, with parameters including a sheath gas flow rate of 30 Arb, auxiliary gas flow rate of 10 Arb, capillary temperature of 350°C, full MS resolution of 120 000, MS/MS resolution of 7500, collision energy settings of 10/30/60 in NCE mode and a spray voltage of 4 kV (positive) or −3.8 kV (negative).
Statistical analysis
The raw mass spectrometry data was converted to mzXML format using ProteoWizard. Subsequently, eXtensible Computational Mass Spectrometry (XCMS) software facilitated retention time correction, peak detection, extraction, integration and data alignment. Lipid identification was performed using XCMS, a custom R program and the lipidblast database. Processed peak area data were imported into SIMCA‐P14.1 software (Umetrics) for multivariate statistical analysis, including principal component analysis (PCA). Lipids with an analysis of variance (ANOVA)
p
< 0.05 in the student's t‐test were considered significant differential biomarkers for group discrimination. The MetaboAnalyst 4.0 Metabolite Enrichment Analysis algorithm (
http://www.metaboanalyst.ca/MetaboAnalyst/
) and lipid ontology enrichment analysis (LION/web) [
19
,
20
] were used to identify the major lipid metabolism pathways enriched among the different groups. Statistical analyses of skin parameters were performed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences software (version 21.0, IBM), employing a two‐sided test with α = 0.05. Continuous variables are reported as mean ± standard deviation, and differences in skin parameter values across groups were determined through one‐way ANOVA or Mann–Whitney test, with
p
< 0.05 considered statistically significant.

INTRODUCTION
The stratum corneum (SC) lipids are a complex matrix that primarily consists of ceramides (Cer), cholesterol, cholesterol esters (CE) and free fatty acids. Additionally, there are minor components, including triglycerides (TG) and diglycerides (DG) [
1
]. SC lipids must maintain the skin barrier function, support skin structure and provide protection against external threats [
2
]. Variations in SC lipid profiles have been associated with various dermatological and systemic conditions, including atopic dermatitis, acne, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis [
3
], hereditary ichthyosis [
4
] and Netherton syndrome [
5
]. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of lipid composition and its variations is crucial for developing effective skincare regimens and therapeutic interventions.
Lipidomics is a powerful analytical tool that involves a large‐scale comprehensive evaluation of lipid metabolism to investigate the relationship between the regulatory network of lipid molecules and the body's symptoms or diseases. Lipidomics has also been applied to study various skin diseases, including sensitive skin [
6
], acne [
7
], atopic dermatitis [
8
], senile pruritus [
9
] and others, and the results indicated the role and underlying mechanism of SC lipids in maintaining skin barrier function.
Furthermore, lipidomic analyses have revealed that age, ethnicity, season, anatomical location and harsh skin cleansing affect SC lipids' composition, organization and dynamics [
10
]. Current research concerning the impact of age on facial skin lipids has primarily been conducted on Western populations [
11
,
12
,
13
]. However, data on the age‐related variations in lipid characteristics among Chinese women are limited. Sebum levels in Chinese women peak between ages 20 and 30 and decline rapidly with age, with a significant moderate intensity correlation between sebum levels and age [
14
,
15
]. Additionally, researchers have found that in Chinese women, the 30‐year‐old stage is a time of onset of ageing characterized by lipid and hormone changes [
16
], along with the emergence of multiple facial ageing features [
17
]. This study collected facial lipids from Chinese women aged 19
–
33 and analysed for SC lipid composition using ultra‐performance liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (UPLC‐MS/MS). The objective was to investigate age‐related changes in key lipids and their associations with physiological parameters.

A comprehensive lipidomic profiling was performed on the facial skin of Chinese women across five different ages (19
–
21, 22
–
24, 25
–
27, 28
–
30 and 31
–
33 years) through an untargeted lipidomic approach. PCA (principle component analysis) is an unsupervised analysis method that reduces the dimension of the data, which can reveal the internal structure of the data, effectively highlighting the overall distribution trends of metabolomics data and the degree of differences between group samples. PCA models were used for multivariate data analysis. The resulting model scores are presented in Figure
2
. The results revealed that the five groups exhibited a significant overlap in the PCA and marginal separations in the positive and negative ion modes, suggesting some inter‐group differences. The interpretation rates for the positive and negative ion models were R
2
X = 0.662 and R
2
X = 0.718, respectively, confirming the PCA model's efficacy in elucidating metabolic differences across varying ages.
FIGURE 2
Scores from PCA illustrate the composition of stratum corneum (SC) lipids across various age groups in both positive (a) and negative ion modes (b). The x‐axis denotes the first principal component (PC1), while the y‐axis indicates the second principal component (PC2). Each point on the scatter plot corresponds to an individual sample, with distinct colours representing different groups. A tighter clustering of sample points suggests greater similarity in the class and content of metabolites, whereas a wider dispersion indicates significant differences in overall metabolic levels.
Significant differential lipids
In total, 1535 lipids species (682 in positive mode and 853 in negative mode) were identified. Among these, 350 lipid species were classified as differential based on ANOVA
p
< 0.05 (Table
S1
).
According to the LipidBlast databases, 350 differential lipids were divided into 20 lipid classes (Table
S2
). With the relative average content of lipids, age‐related changes in individual lipid classes were analysed and plotted in Figure
3a
. Among the 20 lipid classes, CE, hemibismonoacylglycerophosphate (HBMP) and TG exhibited an increasing trend with age, while glycerophosphatidylglycerol (PG) and DG demonstrated a gradually decreasing trend.
FIGURE 3
Thermodynamic diagram of significantly differential lipids (a) and grouped radial bar chart of all Cer across five groups. Thermodynamic diagram (a) displaying data values through colour variations and can be used to visualize matrix situations. They are often used to indicate the expression levels of different substances across various samples, and then patterns unique to different groups can be examined through clustering and other methods. The x‐axis categorizes the various groups, while the y‐axis lists the differential lipids associated with each group. The blocks positioned throughout the diagram reflect the relative expression levels of lipids at their respective locations. The grouped radial bar chart (b) arranges clustered columns radially from a central axis, with each angular sector representing 5 groups. Each Cer subclass is color‐coded, forming clustered bars whose radial lengths quantify subclass abundance across groups. This polar plot architecture enables simultaneous comparison of multi‐subclass spatial‐temporal dynamics in Cer. CAR, Carnitine; CE, Cholesteryl ester; Cer‐ADS, Ceramide alpha‐hydroxy fatty acid‐dihydrosphingosine; Cer‐AP, Ceramide alpha‐hydroxy fatty acid‐phytospingosine; Cer‐AS, Ceramide alpha‐hydroxy fatty acid‐sphingosine; Cer‐BS, Ceramide beta‐hydroxy fatty acid‐sphingosine; Cer‐EODS, Ceramide Esterified omega‐hydroxy fatty acid‐dihydrosphingosine; Cer‐EOS, Ceramide Esterified omega‐hydroxy fatty acid‐sphingosine; Cer‐NDS, Ceramide non‐hydroxyfatty acid‐dihydrosphingosine; Cer‐NS, Ceramide non‐hydroxyfatty acid‐sphingosine; DG, Diacylglycerol; DGTS, Diacylglyceryl trimethylhomoserine; FAHFA, Fatty acid ester of hydroxyl fatty acid; GM3, Ganglioside; HBMP, Hemibismonoacyl‐glycerophosphate; HexCer‐AP, Hexosylceramide alpha‐hydroxy fatty acid‐phytospingosine; HexCer‐NDS, Hexosylceramide non‐hydroxyfatty acid‐dihydrosphingosine; HexCer‐NS, Hexosylceramide non‐hydroxyfatty acid‐sphingosine; PC, Phosphatidylcholine; PE, Phosphatidylethanolamine; PEtOH, Phosphatidylethanol; PG, Phosphatidylglycerol; PMeOH, Phosphatidylmethanol; PI, Phosphatidylinositol; SHexCer, SulfurHexosylceramide hydroxyfatty acid; SL, Saccharolipids; SQDG, Sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol and TG, Triacylglycerol.
Cer constitute a predominant component of the SC lipids, accounting for approximately 50% by weight [
21
]. Cers are structurally characterized by a long‐chain base (LCB) covalently linked to a fatty acid (FA) through an amide bond. LCBs and FAs exhibit structural diversity, including variations in carbon chain length, degree of unsaturation and the position and number of hydroxyl groups. In mammals, LCBs are categorized into five distinct types: dihydrosphingosine (DS), sphingosine (S), phytosphingosine (
P
), 6‐hydroxy sphingosine (H) and 4
E
,14
Z
‐sphingadiene (4,14‐sphingadiene; SD). Additionally, FAs in Cer can be classified into five subtypes: nonhydroxy, α‐hydroxy, β‐hydroxy, ω‐hydroxy and esterified ω‐hydroxy (EO) FAs. Based on the combinatorial diversity of LCBs and FAs, Cers are systematically classified into 25 distinct classes (Table
S3
), reflecting their structural and functional heterogeneity [
22
]. We performed relative quantification of 14 classes of Cer from the SC (ADS, AH, AP, AS, BS, EODS, EOH, EOP, EOS, NDS, NH, NP, NS and NSD) using an internal standard method, including 547 species (Figure
3b
). In the facial SC, NP, NH, AP and AH were abundant (21.9%, 19.7%, 18.5% and 12.0% of total Cer, respectively), followed by NS, AS, NDS and ADS (in descending order, 1%–9%). The proportions of other Cer classes were lower than 1%. The ratio of each Cer class to total ceramides in this study was not significantly different from earlier studies [
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
] (Table
S4
).
K‐means cluster analysis of differential lipids
The K‐means clustering algorithm is an iterative technique employed to cluster data by utilizing distance as a measure of similarity to divide a given dataset into K distinct classes. K‐means cluster analysis was used to investigate the age‐related trends of individual lipid species in Chinese women. The analysis revealed diverse trends in lipid molecules categorized into nine clusters (Figure
4a
). Cluster 2 contained 40 lipid molecules that exhibited increasing relative content with age, while Cluster 8 comprised 51 lipid molecules that gradually decreased. The composition of lipids within each cluster varied significantly (Figure
4b
), suggesting potential co‐regulation or functional relationships among clustered lipids. Furthermore, the relative amounts of DG in the skin of Chinese women significantly diminished with age while CE levels increased. We observed a significant reduction in mean TG chain length with ageing. Sphingolipids displayed acyl‐chain‐length‐dependent changes, with HexCer and Cer in Cluster 8 predominantly containing shorter acyl chains (C18–C23), whereas longer acyl chains characterized sphingolipids in Cluster 2.
FIGURE 4
K‐means clustering analysis of significantly differential lipids (a) and lipid species in Clusters 2 and 8 (b). The horizontal axis represents age groups, and the vertical axis represents the relative content of metabolites after standardization. The cluster represents a group of metabolites with the same change trend, and *metabolite(s) indicates the number of metabolites in that cluster.
Correlation analysis of differential lipids and physiological parameters
The differences in facial skin parameter indicators among different age groups are summarized in Table
3
. The skin hydration, R0, Q0, b* and EI values exhibited almost no changes among the groups. TEWL value increased with age; however, the groups had no significant differences (
p
> 0.05). R2, R5, R7, L*, ITA and MI values, and oil content revealed a decreasing trend with age, and the values in the 19–21 age group were significantly lower than those in the 31–33 age group (
p
< 0.05). The study by Bi et al. [
26
] revealed that for Chinese women with dry skin, the moisture content, TEWL value and oil content of the facial skin exhibited higher levels in the 22–28 years old group compared to the 29–35 years old group. However, statistical analysis exhibited no significant differences between the two groups. In contrast, the L* value, ITA° value and skin elasticity were significantly higher in the 22–28 years old group than in the 29–35 years old group. In terms of the skin moisture content, TEWL value, skin elasticity and skin colour, our research findings align closely with those of Bi et al. However, the oil content results differ from ours. This discrepancy can be attributed to the fact that the research by Bi et al. was confined to the investigation of women with dry skin, which is different from the scope of our research sample.

Biological pathways involved in the association of lipidome with age
All differential lipids were matched with the database to obtain the pathway information of the lipids. Enrichment analysis was performed on the annotated lipid results to determine the primary enrichment pathways of the differential lipids. In total, 91 differential lipids were obtained using MetaboAnalyst, 27.5% of the input lipids were matched with the ontology, and limited lipid pathway analysis was provided. The main characteristic lipid enrichment analysis results are provided in Figure
6a
. Glycerolipid metabolism and phospholipid biosynthesis were primarily enriched with ageing. To identify more precise biological processes and pathways potentially associated with differential lipids, an enrichment analysis was performed using LION/web‐based lipid ontology. The results are presented in Figure
6b
. In the LION/web, 97.52% of the input lipids matched the ontology. The functional enrichment results revealed that one function term, six lipid classification terms and 15 physical or chemical properties terms were statistically significantly enriched in differential lipids. Lipid‐mediated signalling was the enriched function term. The most enriched lipid classification terms included fatty acids (FA), fatty acids and conjugates (FA01), Cer (42:1), Cer (41:1), Cer (32:0) and diacylglycerols (GL0201). The most enriched physical or chemical properties terms were chain‐melting transition temperature (low transition temperature and below average transition temperature), fatty acid unsaturation (a fatty acid with less than two double bonds and saturated fatty acid), headgroup with negative charge, negative intrinsic curvature, contains fatty acid (C14:0, C24:0 and d18:1 [sphingosine]), and fatty acid chain length (fatty acid with 13–15 carbons, 15 carbons, 16–18 carbons and 18 carbons). These results indicate that the inhibition of the FA, Cer (42:1), Cer (41:1), Cer (32:0), and DG changes with increasing age.

DISCUSSION
Multiple studies have reported the variation in facial skin lipid profiles of various skin diseases, sebum levels and age in the Chinese population. However, limited studies focused on the changes in facial skin lipid profiles with age. To the best of our knowledge, this study is the first to investigate differences in the facial skin lipid profile of young Chinese women with age using UPLC‐MS/MS. The study found significant lipid changes with ageing in facial skin and used these differential lipids to identify the biological pathways involved. Additionally, we determined the associations of the differential lipids with skin physiological parameters. These findings provide the basis for understanding the changes in the facial skin lipid profiles of Chinese women aged 19
–
33 and the relationship between lipids and skin physiological parameters.

A total of 1535 lipids were detected, and the screening criteria of ANOVA
p
< 0.05 exhibited significant differential lipids. In total, 350 lipids significantly contributing to the group differences were selected and divided into 20 categories. We found a significant age‐dependent decrease in DG and PG and an increase in CE, HBMP and TG. Besides, Tsugawa et al. confirmed that DG and TG decreased and CE increased with ageing in the mice's ear skin [
27
]. A study on volar forearm lipid profiles of 104 subjects of different ages found that as age increases, there is a significant decrease in TG and DG levels in female skin, while CE levels remain constant [
1
]. However, our findings were contradictory; we revealed that the TG content increased among Chinese women aged 19
–
33. This may be attributed to the skin's characteristics in this age group, which has the highest sebum content [
14
,
15
] and is the stage where multiple ageing features begin to appear [
16
,
17
]. Studies have indicated that Wnt signalling appears to be a marker of skin ageing [
28
]. The activation of canonical Wnt signalling is induced by prostaglandin E2 [
29
]. The increase in triglyceride synthesis triggered by diacylglycerol acyltransferase is accompanied by elevated levels of prostaglandins, including an increase in prostaglandin E2 levels [
30
]. Additionally, studies have reported that TG levels in the tail epidermis of elderly mice significantly increase compared to young controls [
31
].
K‐means clustering was used to analyse further the variation trend of individual lipids with age, which resulted in nine clusters. During the ageing process from age 19 to 33, we observed an increase in the relative content of shorter chain fatty acids associated with TG; however, longer chain fatty acids exhibited a decreasing trend. The relative content of C18:2 in the TG fraction increased by 21% from year 19
–
22 to year 31
–
33. According to the previous report, the values of C18:2 in the TG fraction in hyperkeratotic SC are significantly higher than in normal SC [
32
]. Hyperkeratosis can be triggered by factors associated with photoaging. Therefore, we hypothesized that ageing affects the composition of triacylglycerols in the skin, resulting in chain length and content changes.
The most significant age‐related differences in the Cer composition of the facial skin of Chinese women aged 19
–
33 were the increase of Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0), Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) and the reduction in short‐chain Cer. Skin lacking adequate Cer of the esterified omega subclass concentrations exhibited several hallmarks of diseased skin barriers, including a lack of long periodicity lamellar phase, less ordered lipid packing and increased permeability [
33
]. Increased levels of short‐chain ceramides reduced skin barrier function and permeability in lipid model membranes [
34
]. Overall, the Cer in the facial skin of Chinese women aged 19
–
33 was changing, which improved the skin barrier function and the permeability of the lipid model membrane. Accordingly, the TEWL value of the skin in this age group did not exhibit any significant change. Previous studies have revealed that TEWL decreases significantly with ageing at the cheek [
35
]. Consequently, we believe that changes in ceramide composition and content play an important role in maintaining the stability of TEWL in facial skin for this age group. Besides, we hypothesize that the increase in Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0) and Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) is associated with the proportion of volunteers aged 19
–

). This is because many anti‐ageing active ingredients can increase the level of Cers in the skin.
Pathway enrichment analysis offers insights into the biochemical and signal transduction pathways that can be significantly associated with differential lipid species. The results from the LION‐web enrichment analysis indicated that the enriched functional terms pertained to lipid‐mediated signalling. Lipid‐mediated signalling plays a crucial role in skin physiology and pathology. Lipids, including sphingolipids and oxidized phospholipids, are involved in cellular responses to stress, inflammation and skin barrier function.
Correlation analysis of differential lipids and physiological parameters
The correlation analysis between differential lipids and physiological parameters revealed that skin elasticity was positively correlated with Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0), Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) and HexCer/NDS (d14:0/33:1), and negatively correlated with Cer/AP (t18:0/20:0). Cer is a secondary messenger that plays a central role in the sphingomyelin pathway. Cer stimulates fibroblast cell growth, preventing photoaging‐associated dermal alteration [
36
] and increasing type I collagen expression [
37
]. Moreover, studies have suggested that Cer promotes the formation of collagen fibres and microfibrils, which affect skin elasticity, potentially exerting an anti‐ageing effect [
38
]. However, some studies have demonstrated that Cer 2 inhibits cell proliferation and induces apoptosis in cultured human keratinocytes, possibly via a Bcl‐2‐dependent mechanism [
39
]. Accordingly, different types of Cer could significantly impact their functions: Some can be beneficial for promoting the expression of collagen and fibres, whereas others can cause damage to keratocytes. Additional studies are required to determine the biological functions of Cer with specific structures.
Research indicates that specific Cer can inhibit melanin synthesis in melanocytes by affecting signalling pathways, including extracellular signal‐regulated kinase, and promoting the degradation of proteins like microphthalmia‐associated transcription factor and tyrosinase [
40
]. Subsequently, Cer has a whitening effect. Therefore, the content of Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0), Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) and HexCer/NDS (d14:0/33:1) exhibited a negative correlation with L*‐value and MI (
p
< 0.05).
Study strengths and limitations
This study has certain advantages. First, it is the first to use lipidomics tools to investigate the impact of age on the facial skin SC lipid profiles of young Chinese women. This study provides a theoretical basis for the mechanisms of age‐related skin ageing characteristics by revealing the trend of changes in facial SC lipid profiles during the early stages of ageing. Second, the entire experimental process was subjected to strict quality control. However, this study has some limitations. First, the study population consisted of young individuals aged 19
–
33, divided into five age groups, with 30 samples selected from each group. Therefore, the representativeness of the population is insufficient, and more samples should be included to obtain more comprehensive results. Second, the inherent differences among the volunteers can affect the results of this study. Third, a major limitation is that protein content did not rectify the data. Our sampling method strictly adhered to the sampling procedures reported in the literature. Moreover, the skin patches were weighed and calibrated to reduce sampling errors during SC tape‐stripping and the significant inter‐individual variations in the SC lipid content. Although this standardized sampling method provides our data with a certain degree of reliability, quantitative analysis of Cer and FFA using the protein normalization method can provide a comprehensive understanding of SC lipids' respective contents and changes, and enable comparative studies with other reports. Additionally, many functional studies of lipids are still in their early stages. In the future, it is recommended that the sample size be further expanded to include more age groups and to obtain more accurate results regarding the impact of age on skin lipids. The experimental results must also be comprehensively evaluated with the lifestyle habits of the volunteers.
In conclusion, this article employs lipidomics methods to investigate the impact of age on the facial SC lipid profiles of young Chinese women in the early ageing stage. It analyses the correlation between the two in conjunction with physiological parameters. We demonstrate that among women aged 19–33 in China, 40 lipids increase with age, while 51 lipids decrease with age. The average chain length of DG, TG and short‐chain ceramides decreases with age, while the CE increases. Cer/EODS (d19:0/18:1/O/16:0), Cer/EOS (d28:1/12:0/O/14:0) and HexCer/NDS (d14:0/33:1) correlate positively with TEWL, skin elasticity and brightness, while Cer/AP (t18:0/20:0) exhibits a negative correlation with skin elasticity. This study contributes to a better understanding of the changes in lipid profile composition in young populations and the potential mechanisms of skin ageing.
